Today's quests

Part 1 · Work done by a force
01Lifting bags of wheatFig. 7.2 · why work is force times distance30 XP

A 5 kg bag sits on the floor. To lift it slowly you must pull up with a force equal to its weight, mg. Lift more bags, or lift them higher, and you do proportionally more work. Change both and watch what happens.

Force needed
50 N
Distance
1 m
Work done
50 J
One bag, one metre. This is the unit of comparison for everything else on this slider.

Work done by a constant force is force applied × displacement in the direction of the force, written W = F × s. Its SI unit is the joule (J): one joule is the work done when a force of 1 N moves an object 1 m along the force. Since 1 N = 1 kg m s⁻², a joule is 1 kg m² s⁻².

Say who, and say what
Work is never just "done". It is always done by some force or agency, on some object. Saying "the girl does 20 J of work on the box" is complete; saying "20 J of work happened" is not.
02Positive, negative or zero?Sections 7.1.1 and 7.1.2 · the sign of work35 XP

The sign of the work done by a force depends only on how that force lines up with the displacement. Same direction is positive, opposite is negative, perpendicular — or no displacement at all — is zero.

Pick a case to see the force, the displacement and the sign of the work done.

Now decide each one. Remember: tiredness is not work. Pushing a wall that will not move is exhausting, but the wall is not displaced, so the work done on the wall is exactly zero.

Why carrying a box is zero work
Walking with a box, you push it up to balance its weight while it moves forward. Force and displacement are at right angles, so the work done by your upward force on the box is zero — however heavy it feels.
03Area under the graphFig. 7.4 · work when the force is not constant30 XP

Plot force against displacement and the work done becomes an area. That is useful, because it keeps working even when the force changes as the object moves — where W = F × s on its own would not.

Shape
Rectangle
Work = area
10 J
A steady 10 N over 1 m encloses a rectangle of 10 N × 1 m = 10 J.
Work has no direction
Force and displacement both have magnitude and direction. Work does not. It is described completely by a number and a sign — which is why it can be read straight off an area.
Part 2 · Energy
04The carrom shotExample 7.3 · the work-energy theorem35 XP

Work done on an object shows up as a change in its energy. That is the work-energy theorem: work done on an object = change in its energy. Play the shot and follow the energy from striker to white coin to black coin.

The striker is moving and carries kinetic energy. Play the shot and watch where that energy goes.

At every collision the pair of forces is equal and opposite, so one object gains energy exactly as the other loses it. The striker does positive work on the white coin and the white coin does negative work back on the striker.

A fielder throws a cricket ball at a wicket and the wicket falls. Which statement describes it best?

An object never stores "work" — work is the transfer, energy is what is stored. The fielder's work on the ball became the ball's kinetic energy, and that energy let the ball do work on the wicket.
05Seven forms of energyFig. 7.10 · what energy looks like25 XP

Energy is the capacity to do work, and it turns up in many forms. Match each form to what it is the energy of.

Tap a form, then tap its description.

Forms convert into one another constantly. Electrical energy becomes light in a bulb and thermal energy in a water heater; the chemical energy in your food becomes the mechanical energy of your muscles; a ringing bell turns mechanical energy into sound.

Heat is a transfer, not a store
Doing mechanical work is one way to move energy between objects. Heat is another: put a hot object against a cold one and energy flows from hot to cold, with no contact needed at all when it travels as radiation — which is how the Sun's energy reaches us.
06Kinetic energy benchEq. 7.6 · K = ½mv²40 XP

An object gets its kinetic energy from the work done to set it moving. Starting from rest, W = ½mv², so the energy an object has by virtue of its motion is K = ½mv². Drive both sliders and watch which one matters more.

½ × m × v²
—
Kinetic energy
50000 J
Double the speed
×4
Move the velocity slider and watch the bar. Mass enters once; velocity enters squared.
Why speed limits matter more than kerb weight
Double a vehicle's mass and its kinetic energy doubles. Double its speed and the energy becomes four times as large — all of which the brakes, or whatever it hits, must absorb.
07The ball in the sandActivity 7.1 · U = mgh35 XP

Drop a heavy ball into a bed of loose sand from different heights and compare the craters. The deeper the depression, the more work the ball was able to do — so the more energy it had at the moment of release.

m × g × h
—
Potential energy
20 J
Crater depth
—
A 2 kg ball, g = 10 m s⁻². Raise it higher and you do more work against gravity, so it stores more.

To raise a mass m to a height h you apply a force mg over a distance h, so you do mgh of work. By the work-energy theorem that work becomes stored energy: U = mgh, measured in joules like everything else here.

Stored in the arrangement, not the object
A stretched rubber band, a bent bow and a compressed spring store energy in their deformation. Two separated magnets, two charges, and a ball held above the ground store it in their relative positions. Strictly this is the potential energy of the ball-and-Earth system — but the Earth barely moves, so we call it the ball's.
08Work the numbersExamples 7.2, 7.5, 7.7, 7.10 and 7.1145 XP

Six calculations straight from the chapter. Take g = 10 m s⁻², and watch the signs.

Converting km/h to m/s
Divide by 3.6. So 72 km h⁻¹ is 20 m s⁻¹ and 154.8 km h⁻¹ is 43 m s⁻¹. Every energy formula on this page expects metres per second.
Part 3 · Conservation of mechanical energy
09The falling objectFig. 7.19 · what one form gives, the other takes40 XP

Mechanical energy is kinetic plus potential. Drop an object from rest and watch the two bars: as one shrinks the other grows by exactly as much, and the total never moves.

Potential
100 J
Kinetic
0 J
Total
100 J
At the top: all potential, no kinetic. Release it and follow the trade.

At point A the object has mgh of potential energy and none of kinetic. After falling for a time t it has lost ½mg²t² of potential energy and gained exactly ½mg²t² of kinetic energy. The sum stays mgh the whole way down. When no force other than gravity acts, mechanical energy is conserved.

10The pendulumActivity 7.2 · energy at P, Q and R35 XP

Pull a pendulum bob aside to point P and release it. It swings through the lowest point Q and rises to R on the far side, reaching almost exactly the height it began at.

Position
P
Potential
max
Kinetic
zero
At P the bob is momentarily still at its highest point: all potential energy, no kinetic.

At Q the bob is at its fastest and its lowest: kinetic energy is at a maximum and potential at a minimum. At R it has stopped again and the energy is all potential once more. In a real pendulum, friction at the support and air resistance drain a little each swing, which is why it eventually stops.

11Down the slideExample 7.8 · v = √(2gh)40 XP

Three children of different masses go down three slides of different shapes but the same height. Who reaches the bottom fastest? Conservation of mechanical energy answers it in one line: ½mv² = mgh, so v = √(2gh).

Straight · 20 kg
—
Curved · 30 kg
—
Spiral · 40 kg
—
Same height, three shapes, three masses. Predict before you press.

The mass cancels on both sides, and the shape of the path never enters the equation — only the height does. Ignoring friction, all three arrive at the bottom with the same speed.

The escape ramp
A lorry whose brakes have failed is steered onto a sand-filled ramp. Its kinetic energy has to be turned into potential energy plus work done against the sand. That is Example 7.9 — and it is how a 10-tonne truck at 72 km h⁻¹ is stopped in 20 m without a single brake.
Part 4 · Power
12Up the stairsEq. 7.11 · P = W ÷ t35 XP

Carry your bag up one flight of stairs. Walk it in five minutes or run it in one — the work done is identical either way, because the force and the height are the same. What differs is the rate, and that is power.

Work done
1500 J
Time
10 s
Power
150 W
A 75 kg climber lifting themselves 2 m does 1500 J however long it takes. Slide the time and only the power moves.

Power is the rate of doing work: P = W / t. Its SI unit is the watt (W), and one watt is one joule per second.

Where horsepower came from
When steam engines were new, their output was compared with the animals they replaced. One horsepower is about 746 W. The unit of power itself is named after James Watt, whose engine turned steam into rotation.
Part 5 · Simple machines
13The pulleyFig. 7.24 · mechanical advantage35 XP

A simple machine does not reduce the work a task needs. It changes the size or the direction of the force you must apply. The force you apply is the effort; the force to be overcome is the load; and mechanical advantage = load ÷ effort.

Load
100 N
Effort
100 N
Advantage
1
Lifting straight up, your effort equals the whole weight and you must pull upwards.

A fixed pulley has a mechanical advantage of exactly 1 — it saves you no force at all. What it gives you is convenience: you pull down, using your own weight, instead of hauling upwards. That is why flags are raised this way.

Tick every arrangement that reduces the effort needed — that is, gives a mechanical advantage greater than 1.

14The inclined planeActivity 7.3 · trading force for distance40 XP

A box is too heavy to lift straight onto a lorry, so you push it up a plank instead. Lengthen the plank and the push you need gets smaller — but you push for longer. Watch the two readings move in opposite directions while the third stays put.

Effort needed
500 N
Advantage L÷h
2.0
Work done
1000 J
A 100 kg load raised 1 m needs 1000 J of work, whichever route it takes.

Moving the load up the plank at a steady speed, F′ × L = mgh, so mechanical advantage = L ÷ h. Since L is always longer than h, the advantage is greater than 1 and the effort is less than the weight. Make the ramp longer and shallower and the effort falls further — but the work done never changes.

Why hill roads zigzag
A road that climbs straight up a hillside is a short, steep ramp: very little distance, a very large force. Winding it back and forth makes it far longer and much shallower, so an engine can manage the climb — at the cost of driving several times as far.
15The lever and the seesawActivities 7.4 and 7.5 · F₁d₁ = F₂d₂40 XP

A lever is a rigid bar that turns about a fixed point, the fulcrum. Move the children along the plank until it balances, and see what rule the balanced positions obey.

Left · force × arm
—
Right · force × arm
—
Balance
—
A 15 kg child and a 30 kg child. Find where each must sit for the plank to level.

A lever balances when effort × effort arm = load × load arm. Lengthen the effort arm and a small effort lifts a large load: mechanical advantage = effort arm ÷ load arm. As always, the effort moves further than the load, and the total work is unchanged.

Levers come in three classes, set by whatever sits between the other two. Sort each tool.
